text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
English radical poet and journalist FRANCIS ADAMS was born in 1862. In Queensland, he reportedly told "unpleaseant truths in all sorts of company".
Former South African Prime Minister LOUIS BOTHA, who encouraged reconciliation between the Boers and the British, was born in 1862.
Australian journalist ALBERT DORRINGTON, whose bush stories were serialised in British magazines, was born in 1874.

The eccentric gold-seeker LEWIS LASSETER, who created a legend, was born in 1880. He perished in central Australia in 1931 in the quest for his lost reef of gold. Some are still searching for "LASSETER's Reef".

British actor SIR BERNARD MILES, who had a distinquished career on stage and in films, was born in 1907. He appeared in "Great Expectations" and "In Which We Serve". He also founded the Mermaid Theatre in London.

American actor/director WILLIAM CONRAD, who started his career in radio, was born in 1920. He became internationally known for his television role as 'Cannon' and more recently in the television series "Jake And The Fat Man". He played the "Fat Man", in a manner not unlike a British bulldog.
** EVENTS **
1888 : The legend of 'JACK the Ripper" began. The Central
News Agency in London received a letter signed "Jack the Ripper", with details of the spate of horrific prostitute murders.
1922 : The King of Greece, CONSTANTINE I, abdicated
following the Greek defeat in Turkey.
1930 : American golfer BOBBY JONES completed the
first-ever golfing grand slam when he won the US National Amateur Championships.
1932 : MAUDE ROSE BONNEY landed in Brisbane, becoming the
first woman to fly around Australia. Her trip in the 'DH60G Moth' took 45 days.
1940 : Imperial Japan signed a 10-year economic and
military alliance with nazi Germany and fascist Italy. The Tripartite Pact formalised the Berlin-Rome-Tokyo Axis which began in 1936.
1956 : Television received a warm reception in Australia.

The first service had begun in Sydney two weeks earlier. Melbourne followed with transmission by HSV Channel 7. Hundreds of people blocked city and suburban footpaths in Melbourne to watch the first programmes.
1960 : Europe's first "moving pavement", the travelator,
was opened at Bank Underground Station in London.
1964 : The WARREN Commission found there was no

conspiracy in the assassination of US President JOHN F. KENNEDY. The commission rejected the conspiracy theory, but failed to identify a possible motive for the killing. The report said LEE HARVEY OSWALD had acted alone in the fatal shooting in November 1963. It said that OSWALD's killer, JACK RUBY, was also not involved in any wider conspiracy. The report was critical of the FBI, the Secret Service and the Dallas police force, for poor security.
1968 : One day after the ending of theatre censorship,
"Hair", complete with 13 naked actors, opened in Britain. The brief nude scene was obscured by impressionistic stage lighting. The rock musical's debut was still a big hit.
1973 : The Miss North Australia contestant in the Miss
Australia quest was banned from the competition. Darwin's 17-year-old JUDY GEE was declared ineligible because she was an unmarried mother.
1987 : Australia's WAYNE GARDNER won the world 500cc
motor cycling championship.
1990 : A glamorous British model failed in her bid to get

married. CAROLINE COSSEY undertook a legal challenge to overturn the law that wouldn't let her marry, because on her birth certificate she was declared male. She underwent a sex-change operation in 1975 and was transformed into "TULA", a very successful model. She had appealed against the ruling on the grounds that it breached the European Convention on Human Rights, but the European Court upheld the British law.
1994 : One thousand people were summoned for the jury
pool in the O.J. SIMPSON murder trial, but 700 refused to be considered.
1994 : A state of bushfire emergency was declared in
parts of New South Wales and Queensland, as raging fires continued to burn unchecked across the states.
1994 : The ALP national conference in Hobart adopted a
policy to ensure that women held 35 percent of all winnable seats by the year 2002.
